statements.quote: This chapter is the curated companion to the deep-structure material scattered through the course: **grokking** (memorization-to-generalization, now in the How Algorithms Work lesson), the **wave geometry of transformer layers**, the **isosurface / “truth tunnel”** picture of how probability collapses as context tightens (now in The Foam of Meaning ), and the **group structure of positional embeddings** ( Basic Math IV and Positional Embeddings ).

It catalogues the most striking discoveries researchers did not anticipate from next-token prediction, emergent reasoning, theory of mind, world models, latent knowledge, self-improvement, and the patterns that tie them all together.
LLMs were trained on a single, well-defined objective: **next-token prediction**.
The architecture is a stack of attention layers, the data is text.
Everything else, reasoning, world-modelling, theory of mind, tool use, was not specified, not rewarded, and in many cases not even expected to be possible.
Yet, capability after capability kept *emerging* during scaling.
The sections below catalogue the most striking of these discoveries, grouped by theme, each with a citation to the paper that first reported it and a short note on *why* it was unexpected.
The first major surprise.

(\cite[Brown et al., 2020]{brown2020gpt3}) showed that a 175-billion parameter autoregressive language model could be conditioned on a handful of input-output examples written into the prompt and then continue the pattern on a new query, **without any weight updates, without gradient descent, without a fine-tuning loop**.
This was not how language modelling was supposed to work.
Prior to GPT-3, neural NLP required task-specific architectures, features, and training.
After GPT-3, “prompting” became a programming interface.
The deeper surprise was that the ability appeared *smoothly* with scale: at small scales models ignore the examples, at large scales they exploit them reliably.

**What do the demonstrations actually teach?** A follow-up study replaced the gold labels in the demonstrations with *random* labels and found that performance on many tasks barely dropped (\cite[Min et al., 2022]{min2022rethinking}).
The input-label mapping was not the main thing being learned from the prompt.
What the context supplied was the **task framing**: the format, the label space, the distribution of inputs, and the style of the expected answer.

This is an important correction to the naive reading of in-context learning: the model is not necessarily inferring a new function from the examples, and a prompt can work for reasons that have little to do with the correctness of its examples.

In 2022, (\cite[Garg, Tsipras, Liang & Valiant, 2022]{garg2022incontext}) asked a sharper question: if a Transformer is trained on sequences drawn from a *family* of functions (e.g. linear functions $f(x) = w^\top x$ with random $w$), can it in-context learn a *new* function from that family on the fly?

The answer was yes: at test time, given a few noisy $(x, y)$ pairs, the model produced predictions matching the **optimal least-squares estimator** for that function class, *without ever performing gradient descent at inference*.
The result extended to sparse linear functions, two-layer neural networks, and decision trees, in each case matching or exceeding specialised task-specific learning algorithms.
This established that in-context learning is not task recognition (looking up a similar pretraining task) but genuine inference-time algorithm execution.
If in-context learning is real inference, it must be implemented in some specific circuitry.
statements.section: Induction Heads: The Circuit Behind ICL

statements.quote: (\cite[Olsson et al., 2022]{olsson2022induction}) identified **induction heads**, pairs of attention heads that implement the simple algorithm “complete $[A][B]\dots[A] \to [B]$”.
statements.section: Induction Heads: The Circuit Behind ICL

statements.quote: Across six complementary lines of evidence, they showed that induction heads develop at *precisely the same training step* as a sudden jump in in-context learning ability (visible as a discontinuity in the loss curve).
statements.section: Induction Heads: The Circuit Behind ICL

statements.quote: The implication: many “emergent” capabilities of LLMs may be the macroscopic signature of a small, identifiable circuit forming inside the network.
statements.section: Induction Heads: The Circuit Behind ICL

statements.quote: This is now one of the cleanest examples of *mechanistic interpretability*, explaining a behaviour by finding the responsible weights.
statements.section: Induction Heads: The Circuit Behind ICL

statements.quote: What happens if you give an LLM the *algorithm* for a task instead of examples?

(\cite[Zhou et al., 2022]{zhou2022algorithmic}) tested this on 19-digit addition: a plain few-shot baseline reached 9.5% accuracy; an in-context description of the addition algorithm reached **90.5%**.
The model was not memorising the answers (the numbers were random), not retrieving the algorithm from pretraining (it was given verbatim in the prompt), and not gradient-descenting on the task.
It was *executing* an algorithm it had never seen before, by reading the algorithm from natural-language instructions.
This is a strong empirical anchor for the claim that LLMs can perform general algorithmic computation when the procedure is specified unambiguously.
Through 2018 and 2019, “zero-shot” was almost a dirty word in NLP, you needed either labelled training examples or a very narrowly crafted prompt template.

The **FLAN** paper (\cite[Chung et al., 2022]{chung2022flan}) showed that fine-tuning a model on a *diverse collection of tasks phrased as instructions* produced a single model that could handle thousands of unseen tasks zero-shot.

The surprise was not just the headline numbers, Flan-PaLM 540B reached 75.2% on five-shot MMLU, outperforming the base PaLM 540B by 9.4 points on average, but the *generalisation pattern*: improvements transferred even to *task categories* not represented in the fine-tuning mix (e.g. fine-tuning on English NLI tasks improved performance on non-English reasoning).

Instruction tuning turned out to be a general method for unlocking latent capabilities, much like chain-of-thought later unlocked reasoning: the abilities were there, the model just needed to be told it was allowed to use them.

In a result that foreshadowed chain-of-thought reasoning by two months, (\cite[Nye et al., 2021]{nye2021scratchpad}) showed that a frozen language model could perform multi-step arithmetic, polynomial evaluation, and even the execution of short programs, provided it was given a *scratchpad*: a stretch of tokens to write down intermediate computation steps.
The model was never trained to use a scratchpad; the scratchpad was simply present in the few-shot examples.
The surprise is conceptual: a Transformer has a fixed-width context window, but it can effectively *expand* its working memory by writing into the context window and reading back what it wrote.
The architecture is constant-time, but the algorithm can be unbounded-depth.
This insight, that a language model is in some sense its own computer, is the conceptual seed of everything that followed.

In January 2022, (\cite[Wei et al., 2022]{wei2022chainofthought}) demonstrated that appending *“Let's think step by step”* (or showing worked examples) to a prompt dramatically improves a model's performance on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning benchmarks, sometimes by **more than 50 percentage points**.
statements.section: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Emerges From a Prompt

statements.quote: (\cite[Kojima et al., 2022]{kojima2022zeroshot}) then showed the same effect *without any worked examples*, using only the “magic” suffix.
statements.section: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Emerges From a Prompt

statements.quote: Before this work, the standard assumption was that a frozen language model performs a fixed amount of “reasoning” per forward pass.
statements.section: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Emerges From a Prompt

statements.quote: Chain-of-Thought revealed that the model already contained latent multi-step reasoning capability, it merely needed permission (in the form of the right prompt) to surface it.
statements.section: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Emerges From a Prompt

statements.quote: This finding directly enabled the entire modern reasoning paradigm culminating in o1, o3, and DeepSeek-R1.
statements.section: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Emerges From a Prompt

statements.quote: Once reasoning can be sampled, two natural refinements appeared.

(\cite[Wang et al., 2022]{wang2022selfconsistency}) showed that sampling *many* chain-of-thought traces and taking the majority answer outperforms greedy decoding, on the intuition that correct reasoning paths converge while incorrect ones diverge.

(\cite[Yao et al., 2023]{yao2023tot}) pushed this further with **Tree of Thoughts**: the model generates multiple candidate next steps, *evaluates* each, and decides whether to continue, branch, or backtrack.
On the Game of 24 (a combinatorial puzzle), chain-of-thought GPT-4 solved 4% of problems; Tree of Thoughts solved 74%.
The surprise was not that the model could reason, but that the same model could be coaxed into *deliberate* search and self-evaluation by changes to the inference loop alone.
Until late 2024, reasoning was something the model produced as visible tokens: write a chain-of-thought, then write the answer.
statements.section: Hidden Chain-of-Thought, Emergent Reasoning at Inference

statements.quote: OpenAI's **o1** series and DeepSeek's **R1** (discussed at length in the Reasoning chapter) showed that the same capability can be pushed much further by *lengthening* the chain of thought and rewarding intermediate correctness rather than only the final answer.
statements.section: Hidden Chain-of-Thought, Emergent Reasoning at Inference

statements.quote: The model is allowed (and incentivised) to “think for a long time” before answering, exploring many reasoning paths internally.
statements.section: Hidden Chain-of-Thought, Emergent Reasoning at Inference

statements.quote: The surprise was that *more inference compute* reliably produces *more capability*, even on tasks where the base model has plateaued.
statements.section: Hidden Chain-of-Thought, Emergent Reasoning at Inference

statements.quote: This is the test-time-compute paradigm.
statements.section: Hidden Chain-of-Thought, Emergent Reasoning at Inference

statements.quote: It is one of the few results in deep learning where you can buy better answers with more thinking time, with no additional training.
statements.section: Hidden Chain-of-Thought, Emergent Reasoning at Inference

statements.quote: The mechanism is still poorly understood (we cannot directly observe the model's hidden chain), but the empirical effect is large: o1 jumped several standard deviations on competition math, PhD-level science questions, and code generation compared to GPT-4, with the same pretraining data and a small amount of RL.
statements.section: Hidden Chain-of-Thought, Emergent Reasoning at Inference

statements.quote: A model that answers each fact correctly should be able to combine those facts.
(\cite[Press et al., 2023]{press2022compositionality}) measured this directly using multi-hop questions (“Who directed the film starring the actress who won the 2020 Best Actress Oscar?”).

They found that **single-hop performance improves with scale, but multi-hop performance does not keep up**, the gap between “knows each fact” and “can compose the facts” actually *widens* in the GPT-3 family.
The model *has* the necessary information in its parameters; it simply fails to compose it without explicit prompting.
Chain-of-thought and the “self-ask” method (the model asks itself follow-up questions before answering) close this gap.
The finding is important because it shows that scaling alone does not solve compositional reasoning, and that the right inference-time scaffolding can be the missing piece.
The compositionality gap is a new measurement of an old philosophical objection.

In 1988, Fodor and Pylyshyn argued that **systematicity** — the ability to understand novel combinations of familiar components — comes free in symbolic systems but has to be stipulated in connectionist ones.
A learner who knows “red ball” and “blue cube” should understand “red cube” on first encounter.
Neural networks, the argument went, learn associations, not rules.
The modern benchmark program put the charge to a test.

\citeauthor{lake2018scan}'s **SCAN** benchmark reduced the question to navigation commands and found that sequence-to-sequence models which parsed their training commands perfectly failed to compose the same words into new commands (\cite[Lake & Baroni, 2018]{lake2018scan}).
COGS (\cite[Kim & Linzen, 2020]{kim2020cogs}) reported the same pattern for semantic parsing.

Chollet's ARC widened the frame from language to abstraction itself, proposing that generalization be measured as the *efficiency* of acquiring skill on previously unseen tasks (\cite[Chollet, 2019]{chollet2019measure}).
A compact failure case is the **reversal curse**: models trained on “A is B” routinely fail to infer “B is A” (\cite[Berglund et al., 2023]{berglund2023reversal}).
The model has the fact in one direction and cannot use it in the other — exactly the kind of asymmetry a purely associative account predicts and a rule-based one does not.
The picture is not one-sided.

**Grokking** shows that a memorizing network can continue training into a generalizing one, so memorization and generalization behave as *phases* rather than mutually exclusive outcomes (\cite[Power et al., 2022]{power2022grokking}).

And the sharpest caution about “emergent abilities” is that many of the dramatic curves were artifacts of discontinuous metrics: a benchmark that scores an answer as all-or-nothing can make a smooth improvement in per-token accuracy look like a sudden jump from zero to one (\cite[Schaeffer et al., 2023]{schaeffer2023mirage}).
Whether the remaining gap closes through scale, through search at inference time, or through architectures built around abstraction explicitly is still open.
For decades, code generation was treated as its own sub-field with its own architectures (abstract syntax trees, program induction, neuro-symbolic systems).
Then (\cite[Chen et al., 2021]{chen2021humaneval}) fine-tuned a 12-billion-parameter GPT on GitHub code and produced **Codex**.
On HumanEval, a benchmark of 164 hand-written Python problems, Codex solved 28.8% of problems in a single sample, while GPT-3 (a much larger general LM) solved 0%.

The surprise was twofold: first, that an essentially unmodified decoder Transformer could function as a competent programmer without any architectural changes; second, that **repeated sampling is itself a strategy**, drawing 100 samples per problem and selecting by majority vote or test-case filtering raised accuracy to 70.2%.
The same model, the same weights, but a different inference-time search strategy, and the model becomes competitive with skilled humans on introductory programming tasks.

A surprising empirical finding is that LLMs trained primarily on Python (and English text) can translate code between programming languages reasonably well: Python to JavaScript, Java to Rust, COBOL to Python, even between languages they have seen little of.

The model's code training distribution is heavily skewed (GitHub is roughly 25% JavaScript, 18% Python, 10% Java, much smaller percentages for everything else), but it has seen enough of each language that it can internalise their syntax, semantics, and idiomatic patterns.
Few-shot prompting with examples of the target language style dramatically improves translation quality.
The conceptual surprise is the same as for natural-language translation: the *abstract algorithm* is separable from the *surface syntax*, and the model has internalised the abstract layer.

A capability that emerged from the Codex/Codex-derivative generation of models: given code that fails a test, an LLM can read the error message, identify the bug, and produce a corrected version, often in a single round, sometimes in two or three.

This is *not* trivial: the model has to (a) parse the error message, (b) map it back to the relevant part of the code, (c) hypothesise a cause, and (d) propose a fix that preserves the rest of the program's semantics.
The capability is highly variable (it works much better for simple, well-isolated bugs than for distributed failures) but its existence at all surprised many researchers.
Most pre-LLM code-generation systems had no self-debugging capability; they produced code once and stopped.
The model's ability to read its own outputs, reason about them as *data*, and modify them is the same machinery as scratchpads and chain-of-thought, but applied to code rather than reasoning steps.
LLMs trained on internet text, most of which is *not* game transcripts, can still play simple games surprisingly well.
GPT-4 can play chess at a weak club level, plays Go at a weak amateur level, plays tic-tac-toe and Connect-4 to expert level, and can reason through poker, Mastermind, and Wordle.
None of this was an explicit training target.
The training data contains chess PGN files, Go game records, online game discussions, and (much more recently) generated game transcripts from earlier LLMs.
What is striking is that the same model can play a game it has never been explicitly trained on, simply by being told the rules in natural language and asked to choose moves.

The ability degrades rapidly with game complexity (a strong human chess player crushes GPT-4, and Go is essentially lost at any serious level), but the *existence* of the ability, at all, in a model trained on next-token prediction, was not predicted.
A small but striking capability: given a table of $(x, y)$ pairs sampled from an unknown physical law, frontier LLMs can often produce a closed-form formula that fits the data.

The **AI Feynman** project (\cite[Udrescu et al., 2020]{udrescu2020aifeynman}) showed that automated symbolic regression, working from raw numerical data alone and with no language model, can rediscover dozens of formulas from the Feynman Lectures on Physics, including Hamiltonians, equations of motion, and conservation laws.
AI Feynman itself is symbolic regression, not an LLM.

Separately, LLMs can propose candidate functional forms, which are then fitted and tested; the surprise is that an LLM's training set (which contains physics textbooks, Wikipedia, Stack Overflow) gives it a strong prior over which functional forms are plausible for a given setting.

This is symbolic regression from a language model, no neural network was designed for it, and yet, given a sensible prompt, the model produces something like Kepler's third law or the Gaussian integral.

LLMs trained on broad web text have seen enough cryptography-related material, papers, StackOverflow answers, blog posts, that they can perform a surprising range of cipher-related tasks: encrypt and decrypt messages using classical ciphers (Caesar, Vigenère, simple substitution), implement cryptographic protocols in code, reason about hash functions and Merkle trees, and even invent simple novel ciphers on the fly.

The surprising part is that **classical ciphers are not in the training objective**, the model learned to compute them from examples scattered through its data, and then generalises to unseen cipher parameters.
The capability degrades quickly as cipher complexity increases (modern symmetric ciphers like AES are out of reach), but for toy ciphers the success rate is high.
It is yet another instance of the same lesson: a model that *reads about* an algorithm often learns to *execute* it.
Perhaps the most surprising mechanistic finding of 2022.
(\cite[Li et al., 2022]{li2022othello_iclr}) trained a small GPT on **move sequences from the board game Othello**, the model never saw the board, only the sequence of moves.

Probing the internal activations, they found a non-linear representation of the full board state had spontaneously formed inside the network: each cell's “colour” (black, white, empty) could be decoded from the internal activations — the paper reports an emergent *nonlinear* representation, recoverable with a nonlinear probe.
Causal interventions (artificially flipping a cell's representation) caused the model to predict legal moves as if the board had actually been flipped.
The model had invented a world model because predicting the next move required it.

The lesson: a sufficiently expressive next-token predictor, trained on a sufficiently structured sequence, builds internal representations of the underlying generative process whether or not we ask it to.

As vision models (CLIP, DINOv2), language models (GPT, Llama), and audio models (Whisper, Audio-MAE) scaled independently, researchers expected their internal representations to look different, they were trained on different modalities with different objectives.
(\cite[Huh et al., 2024]{huh2024platonic}) showed the opposite: as models scale, their representations **converge**.
The similarity structure (which images are close to which, which sentences are close to which) becomes more and more alike across modalities and architectures.

The Platonic Representation Hypothesis proposes that there is a single statistical model of reality toward which all large models converge, the way all map projections converge toward an accurate map as their resolution increases.

If true, this would imply that the “universal” representations people intuited were waiting to be found are *forced into existence* by the data alone, irrespective of the architecture that learns them.

A finding that has surprised practitioners over and over again: an LLM trained on diverse internet text can perform well on tasks that look nothing like its training distribution, for instance, classifying bird species from verbal descriptions, parsing legal contracts into structured forms, generating synthetic medical dialogues in a specific style, or producing domain-specific code in obscure libraries.
The mechanism is the standard one, the model has seen enough examples of similar tasks that it can extrapolate, but the *degree* of generalisation is consistently larger than researchers expect.
Studies continue to report larger-than-expected transfer to tasks where the training set contained no examples of the exact task and the model had no fine-tuning.
This is the practical face of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis: the model has internalised general abstractions that transfer cleanly to new domains.
In 2022, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 astonished users by drawing **recognisable pictures using only ASCII and Unicode characters**: a cat, a landscape, a portrait, even a small game of chess.
The model had no image-generation capability (no diffusion, no pixel output).
The drawings were composed of text characters that *look like* the image when viewed at a distance, a llama made of slashes, a face made of colons and parentheses.
Later, LLMs produced correct **SVG** code that, when rendered, generated crisp vector graphics.
None of this is “true” image generation, the model is producing a string of text that *represents* an image.

But the fact that a model trained only on text can perform approximate *inverse graphics*, given “a picture of a cat”, produce text that, when read as visual symbols, looks like a cat, is a striking demonstration of how much world knowledge is encoded in the token distribution.
It is the same world-model finding as Othello-GPT, just projected onto a different modality.

LLMs are overwhelmingly trained on English text, yet they can solve reasoning problems in languages they have seen far less of, and they often solve them *better* when the reasoning trace is in English.

(\cite[Shi et al., 2023]{shi2023cottransfer}) (and parallel work) showed that prompting a model in Bengali or Swahili to “think in English then answer in Bengali” substantially outperforms prompting entirely in the low-resource language.
The internal reasoning and the surface language are partially *disentangled*.
The model has, in effect, an implicit representation of “the reasoning” that is partly language-agnostic.

This is consistent with the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and has practical implications: multilingual chain-of-thought is one of the cheapest ways to improve performance on low-resource languages without ever training on more low-resource data.
For decades, machine translation required parallel corpora: aligned sentences in two languages.
statements.section: Emergent Multilingual Translation Without Parallel Data

statements.quote: Then, around 2020, researchers noticed that multilingual LLMs (mBERT, mT5, GPT-style multilingual models) could translate between language pairs they had never seen paired, for instance, translating from Yoruba to Catalan despite the training data containing no Yoruba–Catalan sentence pairs.
statements.section: Emergent Multilingual Translation Without Parallel Data

statements.quote: The “pivot” happens *internally*: the model encodes Yoruba into a language-agnostic semantic representation and decodes Catalan from it.
statements.section: Emergent Multilingual Translation Without Parallel Data

statements.quote: (\cite[Shi et al., 2023]{shi2023cottransfer}) made the effect measurable by introducing the MGSM benchmark (grade-school math problems translated into 10 typologically diverse languages including Swahili and Bengali); the model solved these problems despite seeing the surface language in only a small fraction of its training tokens.
statements.section: Emergent Multilingual Translation Without Parallel Data

statements.quote: The internal semantic space is, in a real sense, language-independent, exactly what the Platonic Representation Hypothesis predicts.
statements.section: Emergent Multilingual Translation Without Parallel Data

statements.quote: A deeper surprise came from mechanistic interpretability.
statements.section: Latent Knowledge, What Models Know But Don't Say

statements.quote: (\cite[Burns, Ye, Klein & Steinhardt, 2023]{burns2022ccs}) showed that even when a model says something false, its *internal activations* often encode the correct answer.
statements.section: Latent Knowledge, What Models Know But Don't Say

statements.quote: They introduced **CCS (Contrast-Consistent Search)**: an unsupervised method that finds a direction in the residual-stream activation space corresponding to truthfulness, by exploiting the logical constraint that a statement and its negation should map to opposite values along that direction.
statements.section: Latent Knowledge, What Models Know But Don't Say

statements.quote: Crucially, this works even when the model is *prompted to lie*: the latent knowledge is there, intact, and can be extracted without ever sampling a token from the model.
statements.section: Latent Knowledge, What Models Know But Don't Say

statements.quote: The finding reframes hallucinations not as failures of knowledge but as failures of *reporting*, the model often knows better than it says.
statements.section: Latent Knowledge, What Models Know But Don't Say

statements.quote: This is also one of the cleanest pieces of evidence that, internally, language models organise truth along linear directions in activation space, a fact that powers the entire Representation Engineering programme.
statements.section: Latent Knowledge, What Models Know But Don't Say

statements.quote: A surprising and practically important finding.
statements.section: Language Models Know What They Know

statements.quote: \cite[Kadavath et al. (2022)]{kadavath2022selfknowledge} (Anthropic) showed that LLMs can *evaluate their own claims*: given a question, they can produce a calibrated probability P(True) that their answer is correct, even on open-ended generation tasks where there is no single right answer.
statements.section: Language Models Know What They Know

statements.quote: They can also predict **P(IK)**, “the probability that I know”, without reference to any specific proposed answer.
statements.section: Language Models Know What They Know

statements.quote: This is the cleanest form of model *metacognition*: the model tracks, in its own activations, whether it has enough information to answer.
statements.section: Language Models Know What They Know

statements.quote: The same paper showed that P(IK) shifts appropriately when relevant source material is added to the context, and shifts upward when hints are given toward a math problem's solution.
statements.section: Language Models Know What They Know

statements.quote: The capability is far from perfect (P(IK) calibration is worse on out-of-distribution tasks), but the central finding, that the model has a usable internal sense of its own uncertainty, was a surprise.
statements.section: Language Models Know What They Know

statements.quote: This property underlies much of modern LLM-as-a-judge work and selective answering systems.
statements.section: Language Models Know What They Know

statements.quote: A naive expectation would be that each neuron in an LLM corresponds to a single, interpretable concept (one neuron for “cat”, one for “happy”, etc.).

(\cite[Elhage et al., 2022]{elhage2022superposition}) studied toy networks and found that, when the number of features in the data exceeds the number of dimensions in the model, networks store features in **superposition**, sparse linear combinations that pack many features into the same dimensions.
The consequence is *polysemanticity*: a single neuron fires for multiple unrelated concepts (“cat” and “Friday”).
Anthropic extended this finding to real models, (\cite[Bricken et al., 2023]{monosemanticity}) showed that, using sparse autoencoders, the seemingly monosemantic features can be recovered.
The takeaway: the network *is* representing the concepts cleanly; the unit of representation is not the artificial neuron but a *direction in activation space*.
This discovery reshaped the entire mechanistic-interpretability programme.
Theory of Mind, the ability to model that other agents hold beliefs that may differ from reality, was long considered a uniquely human cognitive capacity, emerging around age four.
(\cite[Kosinski, 2024]{kosinski2023tom}) tested 11 LLMs on 40 False-Belief scenarios (640 prompts in total).

The result was striking: smaller and older models solved 0% of tasks; GPT-3-davinci-003 (Nov 2022) solved 20%; ChatGPT-3.5 (Mar 2023) solved 20%; **ChatGPT-4 (Jun 2023) solved 75%**, statistically indistinguishable from six-year-old children.
ToM was not in the training objective; it was not reinforced; it was not a benchmark anyone was optimising for.
It *emerged spontaneously* as a side-effect of language modelling scaling.

The result is contested in detail (subsequent papers find that small prompt perturbations break the ability), but the central finding, that frontier models display systematic ToM behaviour on standard tests, is robust.
The Theory-of-Mind finding of (\cite[Kosinski, 2024]{kosinski2023tom}) was the most visible, but other surprising cognitive abilities have followed.

Frontier models now pass the **false-photo** test (understanding that a Polaroid picture of a previous state can mislead a viewer), the **unexpected-contents** test (predicting that someone opening a candy box labelled “crayons” will be surprised), the **Sally–Anne** variant with nested beliefs, and several irony / sarcasm / faux-pas benchmarks.

None of these tests existed when GPT-3 was trained; none were in the optimisation objective; many were passed at levels comparable to young children by models that were never explicitly taught what a “belief” is.

The mechanisms are still debated (some evidence suggests shortcut pattern-matching rather than genuine mentalising), but the surface performance is a stark departure from the “stochastic parrot” predictions of 2019.
Classical word-embedding arithmetic (*king − man + woman ≈ queen*) was already a surprise in 2013.
The surprise with LLMs is how far this generalises.

Frontier models perform **structural** analogies that have nothing to do with word vectors: given the structure “electron : atom :: quark : ?”, they answer correctly; given “Mitochondria is to cell as chloroplast is to ?”, they answer “plant cell”; given complex metaphors about grief, time, or love, they produce fluent novel metaphors; their quality is not benchmarked.
The training data contains millions of analogies and metaphors, but no explicit instruction to “perform analogical inference”.
The ability emerges from the same next-token objective that produces summarisation and translation.
It is the cognitive operation that humans find most distinctive of “real understanding”, and it was never an explicit target.
Language models famously struggle with exact arithmetic and factual lookup.

(\cite[Schick et al., 2023]{schick2023toolformer}) showed that a model can teach *itself* to call external APIs (a calculator, a search engine, a translation system, a calendar) by a self-supervised procedure: write candidate API calls into text, execute them, keep the calls that *reduce the loss* on subsequent tokens, discard the rest.
The resulting model, **Toolformer**, substantially improved zero-shot performance on a variety of downstream tasks, often matching much larger models.

The surprise was twofold: (a) the supervision signal (loss reduction) was extremely weak, yet sufficient to teach tool use from raw text; (b) the model learned *which* tool to call, *when*, *with what arguments*, and *how to incorporate the result*, all without human-labelled tool-use examples.
For a long time, reasoning and acting were treated as separate LLM capabilities: chain-of-thought for the former, tool-use agents for the latter.

(\cite[Yao et al., 2023]{yao2023react}) showed that the same model can do both at once, *interleaved in a single trajectory*: generate a thought, take an action, observe the result, generate another thought, take another action.

On HotpotQA multi-hop question answering, ReAct over a simple Wikipedia API beat both pure-CoT and pure-acting baselines, because the reasoning traces let the model track what it had already looked up, while the actions let it ground claims in retrieved evidence.
On ALFWorld (household tasks), ReAct beat imitation-learning and RL baselines by 34 absolute points with just one or two in-context examples.

The surprise is conceptual: the same training objective, predict the next token, produces a system that can interleave internal monologue with external tool use, switching modes as the situation requires.
This is the substrate that powers modern LLM agents.

When LLMs are placed in interactive environments (text-based games, web navigation, coding tasks) with the right scaffolding, they exhibit *exploratory-looking behaviour*: visiting unfamiliar states, testing novel actions, and explicitly asking questions to reduce uncertainty.

statements.quote: A long-standing assumption in machine learning was that improving a model's outputs required either better training data or a stronger reward signal.
(\cite[Madaan et al., 2023]{madaan2023selfrefine}) showed that this is not always true.

Using a *single* frozen LLM in three roles, generator, critic, refiner, they ran a loop: the model produces an initial output, then provides natural-language feedback on its own output, then refines the output using that feedback.

Across 7 diverse tasks (dialogue, math reasoning, code generation, summarisation, sentiment reversal, acronym generation, constraint generation), the Self-Refine loop improved outputs by roughly 20 absolute points on average over one-shot generation, even with state-of-the-art GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 as the underlying model.
The implication is uncomfortable for any research programme that treats LLMs as static systems: the model's own assessment of its output is a usable training signal at inference time.
Self-Refine is the conceptual cousin of Constitutional AI, language being used by a model to evaluate language produced by the same model.
A still bolder claim: a model can become a better version of itself without any external supervision.
(\cite[Huang et al., 2022]{huang2022selfimprove}) showed that a 540-billion-parameter PaLM could fine-tune itself on its own Chain-of-Thought traces.

The procedure: prompt the model on unlabeled questions, keep only the answers where the model is highly confident (filtered through self-consistency), then fine-tune on those self-generated, high-confidence rationales.
The result on GSM8K: **74.4% → 82.1%** with no ground-truth labels used at any stage.
The same self-improvement recipe boosted DROP, OpenBookQA, and ANLI-A3.

The constraints are real (you need a base model strong enough that its self-consistency correlates with correctness), but the existence of the effect is striking: a model can be its own teacher, provided it is large enough to grade itself reliably.
Alignment research initially assumed that human-labelled preference data was the only way to teach a model what behaviour was acceptable.

statements.quote: A more troubling surprise.

(\cite[Carlini et al., 2021]{carlini2021extracting}) showed that large LLMs, when prompted with the right prefixes, will emit *long verbatim passages* of their training data, including copyrighted text, personally identifying information, and content that was never intended to be reproduced.
The New York Times sued OpenAI in 2023 partly on the basis of this memorisation.
The phenomenon is not a bug in the usual sense: it falls out of the maximum-likelihood objective, which rewards models for perfectly predicting tokens they have seen many times.
The surprise was quantitative: with the right prompt, hundreds of pages of copyrighted material can be extracted.
It is the cleanest demonstration that an LLM is not “a database with fuzzy retrieval”, it is, in part, an actual database, sitting in the weights.

The Inverse Scaling Prize set out to find tasks on which *bigger models do worse*; the follow-up work (\cite[Wei et al., 2023]{mckenzie2023inverse}) examined those tasks at even larger scale and found that performance on 6 of the 11 tasks is **U-shaped**: it drops up to a point, then rises again.
The U-shape is driven by a phenomenon the authors call “distractor tasks”, patterns in the data that small models follow and that large models eventually learn to ignore.
The lesson: scaling is not monotone.
There are real failure modes of scale, often driven by the model learning surface patterns from human text that are not aligned with what we want.
Whether a given task is U-shaped, monotonically improving, or genuinely inverse-scaling is an empirical question that cannot be answered by extrapolation from smaller models.

In March 2023, a team at Microsoft Research published a 154-page investigation of an early GPT-4 checkpoint titled \textit{Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence} (\cite[Bubeck et al., 2023]{bubeck2023sparks}).

Their central claim was that GPT-4, beyond its mastery of language, could solve novel and difficult tasks spanning mathematics, coding, vision, medicine, law, and psychology, *without needing any special prompting*, and that its performance was “strikingly close to human-level performance” in many of these domains.

The paper documented abilities the authors had not anticipated: synthesising novel proofs, writing functioning code from a one-line description, explaining jokes, drawing ASCII art on request, and passing professional exams such as the bar exam at roughly the 90th percentile.
Whether or not one accepts the “AGI” framing, the paper is a careful catalogue of capabilities that nobody, including OpenAI, predicted when scaling GPT-3.
Taken together, these findings share a common structure that distinguishes them from ordinary engineering progress:
